say.text: A 35-year-old man comes in 6 hours after a flame burn covering 40% of his body.
He is tachycardic and hypotensive, and his haematocrit has risen from 42 to 55.
What type of shock is this?

choices.label: Septic, from infection in the burn
Cardiogenic, from a weak heart pump
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Not septic. Sepsis is tempting because a burn is an open wound and the patient looks unwell.
But a rising haematocrit means the blood is thickening, which is plasma leaving the vessels. Large burns cause that capillary leak.
Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, so the first problem is the lost plasma.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this belief needs the most care: a rising haematocrit in a large burn points to plasma loss, not infection.

say.text: Not cardiogenic. A weak heart is an easy read here because the stem gives you a tachycardic, hypotensive patient.
Some myocardial depression from circulating mediators does occur, but it is an added factor on top of the main problem.
The main problem is the thickened blood and the plasma it has lost, which is the hypovolaemic picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure a weak pump was the cause. The heart is depressed a little, but the main shock type is hypovolaemic.

say.text: Start with the blood, not the pump. A rising haematocrit means the blood is getting thicker.
Ask what has left the circulation before you name the cause.
Yes. Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic: plasma leaks out of the capillaries and the blood thickens.
Myocardial depression from mediators is an added factor, not the main type.

choices.label: Why does plasma leak so fast?

say.text: A local burn releases histamine, prostaglandins and free radicals, which make the capillaries leaky.
The leak is greatest in the first 8 to 12 hours and can continue for up to 24 hours.
Despite some depression of the heart, what is the first-line fluid in the first 24 hours of a large burn?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Ringer lactate is the fluid of choice for burn resuscitation.
Classic Parkland gives crystalloid only in the first 24 hours, with no colloid.
Not inotropes. They act on the heart, and the stem's heart depression pulls you toward them.
Some myocardial depression is real, but burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, so the lost volume is the first target.
Replace the plasma first with Ringer lactate.

sure_note.text: You were sure the heart was the problem. Burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, so volume comes first.

say.text: Not albumin. It is tempting because capillaries leak protein, and colloid appears in other burn formulae.
But classic Parkland uses crystalloid alone at the start. Colloid is considered later, around 8 to 24 hours, when the leak settles.

sure_note.text: You were sure of albumin. Colloid belongs to Evans and Brooke, and to Parkland only later.

say.text: Ask which fluid is the standard for a burn.
Then ask whether colloid belongs in the first 24 hours of classic Parkland.
A forearm burn is mottled red and white. It hurts less than the patient expected, and capillary refill is sluggish.
How deep is it?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Not full thickness. Less pain tempts you there, because full thickness is painless.
But pain is not a depth scale. Deep partial burns also hurt less than normal skin, and they keep a mottled look and sluggish refill.
Full thickness is dry and leathery, white or brown, and does not blanch.

sure_note.text: You were sure that less pain meant deeper. Pain does not run in a straight line with depth; look at blanching and colour too.

say.text: Not superficial partial. Less pain than expected looks like a shallower step, which is the tempting read.
Superficial partial burns are blistered, moist, pink and very painful, and they blanch.
This burn is mottled with sluggish refill, which is the deep partial picture.

sure_note.text: You were sure that less pain meant a shallower burn. Check appearance and refill before you grade by pain.

say.text: Yes. Mottled red and white, less painful, with sluggish refill, is deep partial thickness.
It can take more than 3 weeks to heal, with scarring, and often needs grafting.
Grade the burn by the skin first: its colour, whether it blanches, and how it refills.
Then ask whether the pain agrees with what you see.
Which feature separates full thickness from deep partial thickness?

choices.label: Less painful than the skin around it
Healing takes over 3 weeks, with scarring
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Full thickness is leathery and dry, does not blanch, and is insensate.
Deep partial burns can hurt less, so pain alone cannot separate the two.
Not this one. Pain is the first thing you check at the bedside, so it feels like the separator.
But deep partial burns also hurt less than normal skin, so reduced pain does not separate them.
Full thickness is the insensate one, and it is also dry, leathery and non-blanching.

sure_note.text: You were sure that less pain separates them. Both can hurt less; full thickness is the one that is insensate.

say.text: Not this one. Slow healing is a real feature, and duration is a favourite exam clue.
But it describes deep partial burns, which can take more than 3 weeks with scarring. It tells you the outcome, not what you see on day one.
On assessment, look at colour, blanching and sensation: full thickness is white or leathery, does not blanch and is insensate.

sure_note.text: You were sure healing time separates them. Healing is a later clue; the bedside signs come first.

say.text: Think about what you can see and test on the first day, not what happens by week three.
In the first 24 hours of classic Parkland, what goes into the drip?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Not this one. Albumin is tempting because burns leak protein, and colloid is a familiar part of burn formulae.
Classic Parkland is crystalloid only in the first 24 hours. Colloid is added later, when the leak settles.
The formulae that put colloid into the first 24 hours are Evans and Brooke, not Parkland.

sure_note.text: You were sure Parkland includes albumin. It does not in the first 24 hours; Evans and Brooke carry the colloid.

say.text: Not this one. Dextrose is tempting because some burn formulae add it to the crystalloid.
Dextrose is part of the Brooke and Evans formulae, not of Parkland's Ringer lactate.
Classic Parkland gives crystalloid only, with colloid considered later, around 8 to 24 hours.

sure_note.text: You were sure dextrose belongs to Parkland. It belongs to Brooke and Evans, which also carry colloid.

say.text: Yes. Classic Parkland uses Ringer lactate alone in the first 24 hours, with no colloid.
Colloid and dextrose belong to the Evans and Brooke formulae.
Ask which formula carries colloid in its first 24 hours.
Then ask whether classic Parkland is that formula.
Three working rules for the bedside. Grade depth from colour, blanching and sensation together, because pain alone misleads.
Under-called depth declares itself at 48 to 72 hours, so reassess the burn then.
Simple erythema is not counted in the TBSA for resuscitation.
Which of these statements about the first day of a burn is right?

choices.label: Less pain than expected means full thickness
Under-called depth shows itself at 48 to 72 hours
Give albumin in the first hour, Ringer lactate later
Septic shock first, so antibiotics before fluid

say.text: Not this one. It sounds sensible, because full thickness is painless and the pain scale is easy to read.
But deep partial burns also hurt less than normal skin. Reduced pain does not mean full thickness.
Full thickness needs excision and grafting, so grade it on colour, blanching and sensation together.

sure_note.text: You were sure that less pain means full thickness. Deep partial burns can hurt less too, so pain cannot grade depth alone.

say.text: Not this one. Albumin feels right because burns leak protein, and colloid appears in Evans and Brooke.
Classic Parkland gives crystalloid only in the first 24 hours. Colloid comes later, after the leak settles.
Ringer lactate is the fluid that starts the resuscitation.

sure_note.text: You were sure albumin starts early. In Parkland colloid comes later; Evans and Brooke carry it from the start.

say.text: Not this one. Sepsis is tempting because burns get infected and a septic patient looks unwell.
But first-day burn shock is predominantly hypovolaemic, from plasma loss, which is why the haematocrit climbs.
So the first problem to correct is the lost plasma.

sure_note.text: You were sure the shock was septic. A large burn's first-day shock is predominantly hypovolaemic.

say.text: Yes. Under-called depth declares itself at 48 to 72 hours, so the burn is reassessed then, not only on day one.
Less pain can mean deep partial rather than full thickness, so grade on several signs together.
